questions.question: Which statement about Group 2 compounds and elements is correct? A: BaCO3 is less stable to heat than MgCO3. B: Ba(OH)2 is less soluble than Mg(OH)2. C: BaSO4 is less soluble in water than MgSO4. D: Ba is less reactive with water than Mg.
questions.answer: C - BaSO4 is less soluble in water than MgSO4
steps: Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group, so BaSO4 is far less soluble than MgSO4 (MgSO4 is very soluble).
A is wrong: carbonate thermal stability increases down the group, so BaCO3 is more stable than MgCO3.
B is wrong: hydroxide solubility increases down the group, so Ba(OH)2 is more soluble than Mg(OH)2.
D is wrong: reactivity increases down the group, so Ba is more reactive with water than Mg.
Only statement C is correct.

questions.question: Explain why a warm oven was used to remove water from hydrated magnesium nitrate instead of direct heating with a Bunsen burner.
questions.answer: A Bunsen flame is too hot and would decompose the magnesium nitrate; a warm oven drives off only the water
steps: Magnesium nitrate is thermally unstable and decomposes on strong heating.
A Bunsen flame is hot and uneven, so the nitrate itself could decompose (giving MgO and nitrogen oxides).
A warm oven heats gently, so only the water of crystallisation is lost.
The remaining mass then equals the anhydrous salt, which keeps the calculation of x valid.

questions.question: 5.12 g of hydrated magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO3)2.xH2O, is heated until 2.97 g of solid remains. Calculate x.
steps: Mass of water lost = 5.12 - 2.97 = 2.15 g.
Moles of anhydrous Mg(NO3)2 = 2.97 / 148.3 = 0.0200 mol.
Moles of water = 2.15 / 18.0 = 0.119 mol.
Ratio water : salt = 0.119 / 0.0200 = 5.96, which rounds to 6, so x = 6.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of energy changes, why magnesium carbonate is insoluble in water.
questions.answer: Lattice enthalpy (energy to break the ionic lattice) is much larger than the hydration enthalpy released by water, so dissolving is not energetically favourable
steps: Dissolving first needs energy to separate the ions in the lattice (lattice enthalpy, endothermic).
Water molecules then surround the ions and release energy (hydration enthalpy, exothermic).
Mg2+ and CO3^2- have high charge densities, so the lattice enthalpy is very large.
The hydration energy released is smaller than the lattice energy needed, so the enthalpy of solution is large and positive and the solid stays insoluble.

questions.question: Using the Hess cycle and data provided, calculate the enthalpy change for the thermal decomposition of MgCO3.
steps: Both routes start from the elements Mg(s) + C(s) + 1.5O2(g) and end at MgO(s) + CO2(g).
Direct route: Delta fH(MgO) + Delta fH(CO2) = -602 + (-394) = -996 kJ mol^-1.
Indirect route: Delta fH(MgCO3) + Delta H(decomposition) = -1096 + Delta H.
Equate the routes: -1096 + Delta H = -996, so Delta H = -996 + 1096 = +100 kJ mol^-1 (endothermic).

questions.question: Explain the trend in thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates.
questions.answer: Thermal stability increases down the group because larger cations have lower charge density, polarise the carbonate ion less, and so the C-O bonds are weakened less
steps: Thermal decomposition is MCO3 -> MO + CO2; the cation distorts the carbonate ion, weakening the C-O bonds.
Going down Group 2 the cation radius increases (extra electron shells).
Charge density of the cation decreases, so its polarising power decreases.
Less distortion of CO3^2- means less weakening of C-O bonds, so a higher temperature is needed and thermal stability increases down the group.

questions.question: Four equations for reactions of copper or its compounds are shown in a diagram. Which one is a disproportionation reaction? Options A to D are Reactions 1 to 4.
steps: Disproportionation is when the same element is both oxidised and reduced.
In Reaction 3, copper in Cu+ goes to Cu (0, reduced) and to Cu2+ (+2, oxidised).
Reaction 1: Cu2+ is reduced to Cu+ and I- is oxidised to I2, so two different elements change.
Reaction 2: Cu is oxidised and N (+5 to +4) is reduced, so different elements; Reaction 4 involves no change in oxidation number.

questions.question: Which of the four copper reactions shown in the diagram is an acid-base reaction? Options A to D are Reactions 1 to 4.
questions.answer: D: Reaction 4, CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O
steps: An acid-base reaction is the reaction of an acid with a base, forming a salt and water.
In Reaction 4, CuO (a basic oxide) reacts with H2SO4 (an acid) to give the salt CuSO4 and water.
No oxidation numbers change in Reaction 4.
Reactions 1, 2 and 3 all involve changes in oxidation number, so they are redox reactions.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction of calcium with cold water. State symbols are not required.
steps: Calcium is a Group 2 metal and reacts with cold water to form the hydroxide and hydrogen.
Calcium is oxidised from 0 to +2; hydrogen in water is reduced from +1 to 0 in H2.
Two water molecules are needed so that one Ca(OH)2 (two OH- ions) and one H2 are formed.
Balanced equation: Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2.

questions.question: Explain why a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide is more alkaline than a saturated solution of magnesium hydroxide.
questions.answer: Ca(OH)2 is more soluble than Mg(OH)2, so a saturated Ca(OH)2 solution contains a higher concentration of OH- ions
steps: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.
Calcium hydroxide dissolves to a greater extent than magnesium hydroxide at the same temperature.
So a saturated calcium hydroxide solution has a higher [OH-].
Higher [OH-] means a higher pH, so the calcium hydroxide solution is more alkaline.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation for the formation of the gas when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a solution containing carbonate ions. State symbols are not required.
steps: Carbonate ions react with acid, H+ ions, to form carbon dioxide gas.
The carbonate ion takes two H+ ions: CO3^2- + 2H+.
The products are CO2 gas and water, H2O.
Ionic equation: CO3^2- + 2H+ -> CO2 + H2O.

questions.question: Write the equation for the formation of the white precipitate when the gas is bubbled through limewater. Include state symbols.
steps: Limewater is aqueous calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2(aq).
Carbon dioxide gas reacts with it to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which is the white precipitate.
Water is also formed.
Equation with state symbols: Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l).

questions.question: Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O. Calculate the minimum mass of magnesium hydroxide needed to neutralise 0.150 mol of hydrochloric acid. Give the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
steps: From the equation, 2 mol HCl react with 1 mol Mg(OH)2.
Moles of Mg(OH)2 = 0.150 / 2 = 0.0750 mol.
Mass = 0.0750 x 58.3 = 4.37 g, to 3 significant figures (matching 0.150).

questions.question: 50.0 cm3 of 2.00 mol dm-3 nitric acid reacts exactly with 50.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 barium hydroxide to form neutral barium nitrate solution. What is the concentration of barium nitrate? A 0.05, B 0.50, C 1.00, D 2.00 (mol dm-3).
steps: Equation: 2HNO3 + Ba(OH)2 -> Ba(NO3)2 + 2H2O, so moles Ba(NO3)2 = 0.0500 mol.
Concentration = 0.0500 / 0.100 = 0.50 mol dm-3.

questions.question: Each burette reading has an uncertainty of +/- 0.05 cm3. What is the percentage uncertainty in measuring 50.00 cm3 of nitric acid? A +/-0.40%, B +/-0.20%, C +/-0.10%, D +/-0.05%.
steps: Measuring a volume with a burette uses two readings (start and end).
Total uncertainty = 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.10 cm3.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.10 / 50.00 x 100 = 0.20%.
Answer B.

questions.question: Complete a dot-and-cross diagram showing a possible arrangement of the outer shell electrons in a molecule of sulfur dioxide (dots for sulfur, crosses for oxygen).
questions.answer: S bonded to each O by a double bond (two shared pairs each); one lone pair on S; each O has two lone pairs. Total 18 outer electrons
steps: Count outer electrons: S has 6, each O has 6, so SO2 has 18 outer electrons.
Form two S=O double bonds, each with two shared pairs (4 electrons), using 8 electrons in total.
Put the remaining 2 electrons on sulfur as one lone pair.
Give each oxygen two lone pairs to complete its octet; 8 + 2 + 8 = 18 electrons.
Draw sulfur electrons as dots and oxygen electrons as crosses, with shared pairs shown as overlapping dots and crosses.

questions.question: Suggest a value for the bond angle in a molecule of sulfur dioxide.
questions.answer: About 119-120 degrees (less than 120 degrees because of the lone pair)
steps: Sulfur in SO2 has three electron regions: two bonding regions and one lone pair.
Three regions give a trigonal planar arrangement, with ideal angle 120 degrees.
The lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly, so the O-S-O angle is slightly less than 120 degrees.
Suggested value: about 119-120 degrees.

questions.question: Give a reason why a further titration was not attempted. The titre results are in a table in the PDF.
questions.answer: Titres 2 and 3 (21.15 and 21.05 cm3) are concordant, within 0.10 cm3 of each other
steps: Titration 1 (21.55 cm3) is the rough result and differs from the others by more than 0.10 cm3.
Titrations 2 and 3 (21.15 and 21.05 cm3) agree to within 0.10 cm3, so they are concordant.
The mean titre of 21.10 cm3 is the mean of these two concordant values, so no further titration was needed.

questions.question: Solution Z (40.0 cm3) is titrated in 10.0 cm3 portions with 0.00500 mol dm-3 NaOH; the mean titre is 21.10 cm3. Equation 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O. Calculate the moles of sulfuric acid in the 40 cm3 of solution Z.
steps: Moles NaOH in one titre = 0.00500 x 0.02110 = 1.055 x 10^-4 mol.
From 2NaOH : 1 H2SO4, moles H2SO4 in 10.0 cm3 = 1.055 x 10^-4 / 2 = 5.275 x 10^-5 mol.
The 40.0 cm3 of solution Z is 4 times the 10.0 cm3 portion.

questions.question: Using the answer to (b)(ii) and the equation SO2(g) + H2O2(aq) -> H2SO4(aq), deduce the moles of sulfur dioxide that were bubbled through the hydrogen peroxide.
steps: The equation SO2 + H2O2 -> H2SO4 has a 1:1 mole ratio.
All the SO2 is converted to H2SO4, so moles of SO2 = moles of H2SO4.
Moles SO2 = 2.11 x 10^-4 mol.

questions.question: Air is bubbled through hydrogen peroxide at 10 dm3 min-1 for 30 minutes. Calculate the concentration of sulfur dioxide in the air in ppm by volume. Molar volume at r.t.p. = 24 dm3 mol-1.
steps: Volume of air = 10 dm3 min-1 x 30 min = 300 dm3.
Moles SO2 = 2.11 x 10^-4 mol (from (b)(iii)); volume SO2 = 2.11 x 10^-4 x 24 = 5.06 x 10^-3 dm3.
ppm by volume = 1.69 x 10^-5 x 10^6 = 16.9 ppm.

questions.question: Chlorine free radicals react with ozone. Derive the overall equation for this reaction of ozone. State symbols are not required.
steps: Add the two steps: Cl + O3 + ClO + O3 -> ClO + O2 + Cl + 2O2.
Cl and ClO appear on both sides, so they cancel (Cl is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst).
What is left: 2O3 -> 3O2.

questions.question: Give two reasons why a small number of chlorine free radicals in the upper atmosphere causes a large decrease in the amount of ozone.
questions.answer: The Cl radical is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst; each Cl radical can destroy many thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction
steps: Chlorine radicals are regenerated at the end of each cycle, so they are not used up.
They act as a catalyst, so a small number of radicals can keep removing ozone.
Each radical can react with many ozone molecules before it is removed, so the chain is long.
Together these reasons explain the large decrease in ozone.

questions.question: Show, using all relevant oxidation numbers, that 2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g) is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: S is oxidised from +4 to +6; O is reduced from 0 to -2 (so it is a redox reaction)
steps: In SO2: S = +4 (O is -2 each, so S = +4); in SO3: S = +6.
S changes from +4 to +6, an increase, so sulfur is oxidised.
In O2 each O = 0; in SO3 each O = -2, a decrease, so oxygen is reduced.
Both oxidation and reduction occur, so the reaction is redox.

questions.question: Draw an enthalpy level diagram for SO3(g) + H2O(l) -> H2SO4(aq), with deltaH = -200 kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: Reactants SO3(g) + H2O(l) on a higher level; H2SO4(aq) 200 kJ mol-1 lower; downward arrow labelled deltaH = -200 kJ mol-1
steps: The reaction is exothermic (deltaH is negative), so the products are at a lower enthalpy level than the reactants.
Draw the reactant level for SO3(g) + H2O(l) as the higher line.
Draw the product level for H2SO4(aq) 200 kJ mol-1 below it.
Add a downward arrow between the levels labelled deltaH = -200 kJ mol-1.

questions.question: Assess the effect of both carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide released in the 1815 Indonesian eruption on global temperatures, given that global low temperatures followed the next year.
questions.answer: CO2 is a greenhouse gas and warms the Earth slightly, but sulfur dioxide forms reflective sulfuric acid droplets that cool the Earth more strongly; the overall effect was cooling
steps: CO2 is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs infrared radiation and causes a small warming effect.
SO2 forms sulfuric acid droplets that reflect UV and sunlight back into space.
This reduces the energy reaching the lower atmosphere, which cools the Earth.
The cooling effect of the sulfuric acid droplets is much larger than the warming from CO2 over this short time, so the overall effect was global cooling.

questions.question: Which of these sulfates is least soluble in water? A CaSO4, B BaSO4, C K2SO4, D Rb2SO4.
steps: Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group: MgSO4 > CaSO4 > SrSO4 > BaSO4.
BaSO4 is the least soluble Group 2 sulfate and is used as an insoluble test for sulfate ions.
K2SO4 and Rb2SO4 (Group 1 sulfates) are soluble.
Answer B.

questions.question: Write the equation for the formation of the white precipitate in the limewater test for carbon dioxide. Include state symbols.
steps: Limewater is aqueous calcium hydroxide.
CO2 gas reacts with it to form insoluble calcium carbonate, the white solid.
Water is the other product.
Equation: Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l).

questions.question: 25.0 cm3 portions of saturated calcium hydroxide were titrated with 0.0500 mol dm-3 HCl (mean titre 23.40 cm3, phenolphthalein indicator). Calculate the concentration of calcium hydroxide in g dm-3. Mr(Ca(OH)2) = 74.1.
steps: Equation Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + 2H2O, so moles Ca(OH)2 in 25.0 cm3 = 1.170 x 10^-3 / 2 = 5.850 x 10^-4 mol.
Concentration = 5.850 x 10^-4 / 0.0250 = 0.0234 mol dm-3.
Mass concentration = 0.0234 x 74.1 = 1.73 g dm-3 (3 s.f.).

questions.question: The titration is repeated using a saturated solution of magnesium hydroxide. Explain the difference (if any) in the mean titre.
questions.answer: The mean titre is smaller, because magnesium hydroxide is much less soluble, so its saturated solution contains a lower concentration of OH- ions
steps: Magnesium hydroxide is far less soluble than calcium hydroxide.
A saturated Mg(OH)2 solution therefore has a much lower [OH-] than a saturated Ca(OH)2 solution.
Less acid is needed to neutralise the same volume of the less concentrated alkali.
So the mean titre with magnesium hydroxide is smaller.

questions.question: Compound Q gives off nitrogen dioxide when heated and gives a red flame test. Which compound could be Q? A barium nitrate, B lithium nitrate, C magnesium nitrate, D rubidium nitrate.
steps: Lithium is the only Group 1 nitrate that decomposes to NO2: 4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2.
Other Group 1 nitrates form nitrites and O2 instead, so rubidium nitrate does not give NO2.
Lithium gives a red flame, and barium gives green, so only lithium fits both clues.
Answer B.

questions.question: Which colour and test results are correct for nitrogen dioxide gas? Options are shown in a table in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: brown, damp litmus paper turns from blue to red
steps: Nitrogen dioxide, NO2, is a brown gas.
It is an acidic gas: it reacts with water in damp litmus paper to form acids (HNO3 and HNO2).
Acid turns blue litmus red, so the colour change is blue to red: option A.

questions.question: In an oxide of potassium the oxidation number of oxygen is -1/2. What is the formula of this oxide? A K2O, B K2O2, C K2O3, D KO2.
steps: Potassium is Group 1, so K is +1 in all its compounds.
For the oxygen to be -1/2, the compound must contain O2 units with total oxidation number -1 per O2 pair.
Test KO2: K +1 + 2 x (-1/2) = 0, which balances.
Answer D (potassium superoxide).

questions.question: A 6.0 g sample of MgC2O4 decomposes to MgCO3 and CO (MgC2O4 -> MgCO3 + CO) and is 70% complete after heating. Calculate the total mass of solid remaining.
steps: 70% decomposed: moles decomposed = 0.70 x 0.0534 = 0.0374 mol; moles CO produced = 0.0374 mol.
Mass of CO lost = 0.0374 x 28.0 = 1.05 g, so solid remaining = 6.0 - 1.05 = 4.95 g.
Check: MgCO3 formed (0.0374 mol x 84.3 = 3.15 g) plus unreacted MgC2O4 (0.0160 mol x 112.3 = 1.80 g) gives 4.95 g.

questions.question: Describe and explain the trend in thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates going down the group.
questions.answer: Thermal stability increases down the group, so a higher temperature is needed; larger cations have lower charge density and polarise the carbonate ion less
steps: Describe: going down Group 2, carbonates need a higher temperature to decompose.
Explain: cation size increases down the group, so the charge density of the cation falls.
A cation of lower charge density polarises the carbonate ion less, so C-O bonds are weakened less.
Less distortion means decomposition needs more heat, so thermal stability increases down the group.

questions.question: Suggest why a pure sample of magnesium carbonate will not be produced from the decomposition of magnesium oxalate even if the sample is heated for longer.
questions.answer: At the temperature needed, MgCO3 also begins to decompose to MgO and CO2, so the solid becomes a mixture with MgO
steps: Heating for longer or to a higher temperature gives more energy to the reaction.
Magnesium carbonate itself decomposes on stronger heating: MgCO3 -> MgO + CO2.
So some MgCO3 is converted to MgO as heating continues.
The product is therefore a mixture containing MgO, not pure MgCO3.

questions.question: A pellet of sodium hydroxide has mass 0.700 g (Mr NaOH = 40). Pellets were dissolved to make 350 cm3 of 0.25 mol dm-3 solution. How many pellets were dissolved? A 4, B 5, C 8, D 125.
steps: Moles NaOH = 0.25 x 0.350 = 0.0875 mol.
Mass NaOH = 0.0875 x 40 = 3.50 g.
Number of pellets = 3.50 / 0.700 = 5.
Answer B.

questions.topic: Moles Of Sulfuric Acid In Titration
questions.question: 25.0 cm3 of the NaOH solution from (a) (0.25 mol dm-3) was titrated with sulfuric acid, 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O. Calculate the moles of sulfuric acid that reacted. A 0.0031, B 0.0063, C 0.013, D 0.044.
steps: Moles NaOH in 25.0 cm3 = 0.25 x 0.0250 = 0.00625 mol.
Mole ratio 2NaOH : 1 H2SO4, so moles H2SO4 = 0.00625 / 2 = 0.003125 mol.
Rounded to 2 s.f., this is 0.0031 mol.
Answer A.

questions.question: Phenolphthalein was used in the titration of NaOH (in the flask) with sulfuric acid. What was the colour change at the endpoint? A colourless to pink, B pink to colourless, C orange to yellow, D yellow to orange.
steps: Phenolphthalein is pink in alkaline solution.
The flask contains NaOH, so the solution starts pink.
At the endpoint all the alkali is neutralised and the solution becomes acidic or neutral, so it turns colourless.
Answer B.

questions.question: Minimum volume of 0.100 mol dm-3 BaCl2 needed to precipitate all the sulfate ions in 200 cm3 of 0.05 mol dm-3 Ga2(SO4)3. A 100 cm3, B 200 cm3, C 300 cm3, D 400 cm3.
steps: Each formula unit gives 3 sulfate ions, so moles SO4^2- = 0.0300 mol.
Ba2+ : SO4^2- is 1:1, so moles BaCl2 needed = 0.0300 mol.

questions.question: Which compound gives no colour in a flame test and produces an alkaline gas when warmed with NaOH? A Ca(OH)2, B Mg(OH)2, C NH4Cl, D BeCl2.
steps: Warming NH4Cl with NaOH releases ammonia gas, which is alkaline.
Ammonium salts give no flame colour because NH4+ contains no metal ion.
Ca(OH)2 gives a brick-red flame and does not release ammonia.
Answer C.

questions.question: Describe two observations when a small amount of solid sodium carbonate is added to an aqueous acid such as ethanoic acid.
questions.answer: Effervescence (fizzing) as CO2 gas is given off, and the solid dissolves or disappears
steps: Sodium carbonate reacts with an acid to release carbon dioxide gas.
Observation 1: the mixture fizzes or bubbles (effervescence).
Observation 2: the solid carbonate dissolves or gets smaller as it reacts.
These two observations confirm the presence of an acid.

questions.question: CH3COONa(aq) + 3H2O(l) -> CH3COONa.3H2O(s), deltaH = -19.7 kJ mol-1. A hand warmer of mass 63.2 g forms 20.1 g of hydrated sodium ethanoate. Specific heat capacity = 3.0 J g-1 C-1. Initial temperature 5.0 C. Calculate the maximum temperature.
steps: Moles of hydrate formed = 20.1 / 136.0 = 0.148 mol.
Energy released = 0.148 x 19.7 kJ = 2.91 kJ = 2910 J (the crystallisation is exothermic).
Temperature rise = q / (m x c) = 2910 / (63.2 x 3.0) = 15.4 C.
Maximum temperature = 5.0 + 15.4 = 20.4 C.

questions.question: Calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction of pure ethanoic acid with ammonium carbonate to form ammonium ethanoate by completing a Hess cycle, using the data shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: +57.0 kJ mol^-1 (for 2CH3COOH + (NH4)2CO3, as the equation is written)
steps: Equation: 2CH3COOH(l) + (NH4)2CO3(s) -> 2CH3COONH4(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(l). Put the reactants in the top left box, the products in the top right box, and the elements (5C + 8H2 + N2 + 3.5O2) in the bottom box, with arrows up to both.
Sum of Delta fH(reactants) = 2(-484.5) + (-939.9) = -1908.9 kJ mol^-1.
Delta rH = sum of Delta fH(products) - sum of Delta fH(reactants) = -1851.9 - (-1908.9) = +57.0 kJ mol^-1.
Per mole of ethanoic acid this is +28.5 kJ mol^-1.

questions.question: A cleaning solution contains no more than 1.8 g of ammonium carbonate, (NH4)2CO3, in 100 cm3 of solution. Calculate the maximum concentration in mol dm-3.
steps: Mass per dm3 = 1.8 g x 10 = 18 g dm-3.
Moles per dm3 = 18 / 96.0 = 0.188 mol dm-3.
To 2 significant figures (matching 1.8 g), the maximum concentration is 0.19 mol dm-3.

questions.question: Write the equation for the reaction of potassium with cold water to form potassium hydroxide and hydrogen. Include state symbols.
steps: Potassium reacts with water to form KOH and hydrogen gas.
Balance K: 2 K on each side; balance H and O with 2 H2O on the left.
Products: 2KOH(aq) (soluble) and H2(g).
Equation: 2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g).

questions.question: The reaction of potassium with water is a redox reaction. State which element is oxidised and which is reduced, and justify with initial and final oxidation numbers.
questions.answer: Potassium is oxidised (0 to +1); hydrogen is reduced (+1 in H2O to 0 in H2)
steps: Potassium starts as an element, so its oxidation number is 0, and ends as K+ in KOH, so +1.
An increase in oxidation number means K is oxidised.
Hydrogen starts as +1 in H2O and ends as 0 in H2.
A decrease in oxidation number means H is reduced.

questions.question: The reaction of potassium with water is vigorous and a flame is seen. State the colour of the flame.
steps: Potassium compounds give a lilac or purple flame.
The flame seen during the reaction is due to the potassium ions emitting light as electrons drop to lower energy levels.
So the flame colour is lilac.

questions.question: A titration of MOH(aq) with hydrochloric acid (0.400 mol dm-3) uses phenolphthalein. State the colour change at the end-point.
steps: The conical flask contains the alkali MOH with phenolphthalein, so the solution is pink.
Hydrochloric acid is added from the burette until the solution is neutralised.
At the endpoint the solution is no longer alkaline, so it becomes colourless.
Colour change: pink to colourless.

questions.question: Using the mass of metal M and the titration results with 0.400 mol dm-3 HCl (250.0 cm3 volumetric flask, 25.0 cm3 aliquots), calculate the relative atomic mass of M and identify M.
questions.answer: Ar of M is about 7.2, so M is lithium
steps: Moles of HCl in the mean titre = 0.01280 dm3 x 0.400 mol dm-3 = 5.12 x 10^-3 mol.
MOH : HCl is 1 : 1, so 25.0 cm3 of solution contains 5.12 x 10^-3 mol MOH.
The whole 250.0 cm3 contains 10 x this = 5.12 x 10^-2 mol, which equals the moles of M (1 mol M gives 1 mol MOH).
Ar = mass / moles = 0.37 / 0.0512 = 7.2, which is closest to lithium (6.9), so M is Li.

questions.topic: Effect Of Oil On Relative Mass
questions.question: Another student did not wipe the oil off the metal before weighing it. State how this changes the calculated relative atomic mass of M and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The calculated Ar is too high, because the measured mass includes the mass of oil while the moles from the titration are unchanged
steps: Ar = mass of M / moles of M.
The moles of M found from the titration are unaffected by the oil.
The weighed mass includes the mass of the oil, so it is larger than the true mass of metal.
A larger mass for the same moles gives a larger calculated Ar, so the value is too high.

questions.question: What volume of hydrogen gas is produced when 3.00 g of lithium reacts with water at r.t.p. (2Li + 2H2O -> 2LiOH + H2; molar volume 24.0 dm3 mol-1)? A 0.217, B 0.435, C 5.22, D 10.4 (dm3).
steps: From 2Li : 1 H2, moles H2 = 0.435 / 2 = 0.217 mol.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which factors explain the decrease in ionisation energy as Group 1 is descended? I protons increase; II outer electron further from nucleus; III shielding increases; IV unpaired outer electrons increase. A I and II, B II and III, C III and IV, D I, II, III and IV.
steps: Going down Group 1 more electron shells are added, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus (II).
More inner shells mean more shielding (III), which reduces the attraction on the outer electron.
The number of protons increases (I), but this is outweighed by the extra shells and shielding, so it does not explain the decrease.
Unpaired electrons (IV) are not the cause; answer B.

questions.question: 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2. What is the total volume of gas formed at r.t.p. when 0.005 mol of Mg(NO3)2 decomposes completely? Molar volume 24 000 cm3 mol-1. A 600, B 300, C 240, D 120 (cm3).
steps: 2 mol Mg(NO3)2 give 4 mol NO2 + 1 mol O2 = 5 mol gas.
So 1 mol Mg(NO3)2 gives 2.5 mol gas.
0.005 mol Mg(NO3)2 gives 0.005 x 2.5 = 0.0125 mol gas.
Volume = 0.0125 x 24 000 = 300 cm3; answer B.

questions.question: A 4.00 mol dm-3 acid is diluted to make 150 cm3 of 0.35 mol dm-3 solution. What volume of water is required? A 13.1 cm3, B 52.5 cm3, C 97.5 cm3, D 136.9 cm3.
steps: Volume of concentrated acid = (0.35 x 150) / 4.00 = 13.1 cm3.
Water needed = final volume - acid volume = 150 - 13.1 = 136.9 cm3.
Answer D.

questions.question: Data for Group 1 and Group 2 cations W, X, Y and Z are shown in a table. Which cation would form the nitrate with the greatest thermal stability? A W, B X, C Y, D Z.
steps: Thermal stability of a nitrate is greater when the cation is less polarising, so it distorts the nitrate ion less.
Polarising power rises with charge density (high charge, small radius).
Z has the lowest charge (+1) and the largest radius (0.149 nm), so it has the lowest charge density.
X also has +1 but a smaller radius; W and Y are +2, so they are more polarising. So Z gives the most stable nitrate.

questions.question: Which property decreases as Group 2 is descended? A reactivity of the elements, B solubility of the hydroxides, C solubility of the sulfates, D thermal stability of the carbonates.
steps: Reactivity increases down Group 2.
Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2.
Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2 (BaSO4 is least soluble).
Carbonate thermal stability increases down Group 2. Answer C.

questions.question: Two titrations of NaOH (in the flask) with HCl (in the burette) use methyl orange and phenolphthalein respectively. What are the colour changes at the end-points? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: methyl orange yellow to orange; phenolphthalein pink to colourless
steps: The flask contains NaOH (alkaline) and acid is added from the burette.
Methyl orange is yellow in alkali and turns orange at the end-point (red only in excess acid).
Phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and turns colourless at the end-point.
So the correct row is B.

questions.question: State why the thermal decomposition of magnesium ethanedioate should be carried out in a fume cupboard.
questions.answer: Carbon monoxide, a toxic gas, is produced
steps: MgC2O4 decomposes to MgCO3 and carbon monoxide, CO.
Carbon monoxide is toxic, so it must be removed from the laboratory air.
A fume cupboard removes the gas safely.

questions.question: After heating a 6.0 g sample of magnesium ethanedioate for three minutes, the decomposition is 70% complete. Calculate the total mass of the solid mixture that remains.
steps: 70% decomposed: moles decomposed = 0.0374 mol, producing 0.0374 mol CO.
Mass of CO lost = 0.0374 x 28.0 = 1.05 g, so solid remaining = 6.0 - 1.05 = 4.95 g.
Check: MgCO3 (0.0374 x 84.3 = 3.15 g) plus unreacted MgC2O4 (0.0160 x 112.3 = 1.80 g) gives 4.95 g.

questions.question: Magnesium carbonate decomposes at a higher temperature than magnesium ethanedioate (MgCO3 -> MgO + CO2). Explain the trend in thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates going down the group.
questions.answer: Thermal stability increases down the group: larger cations have lower charge density and polarise the carbonate ion less, so more heat is needed
steps: Going down Group 2 the cation gets larger.
Its charge density falls, so it polarises the carbonate ion less.
The C-O bonds in CO3^2- are weakened less, so a higher temperature is needed.
Thermal stability therefore increases down the group.

questions.question: Which is the ionic equation for the reaction of solid barium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid? Options are in the PDF.
steps: Solid barium carbonate is insoluble, so it stays as BaCO3(s) in the ionic equation.
Hydrochloric acid is fully ionised, giving H+(aq) (Cl- is a spectator ion and is left out).
The products are Ba2+(aq) (BaCl2 is soluble), CO2(g) and H2O(l), and 2H+ are needed to balance.
B has wrong formulae (Ba2CO3, Ba+); C shows a free carbonate ion as a solid, which is wrong; D shows HCl(aq) as undissociated molecules and has no barium ion.

questions.question: Which nitrate forms oxygen as its only gaseous product on heating? A LiNO3, B NaNO3, C Mg(NO3)2, D Ca(NO3)2.
steps: Group 1 nitrates (except lithium) decompose to the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2.
So sodium nitrate gives only O2 as a gas.
LiNO3, Mg(NO3)2 and Ca(NO3)2 all give NO2 as well as O2.
Answer B.

questions.question: A small piece of calcium is added to distilled water. Which is the equation for this reaction? A Ca + H2O -> CaO + H2, B Ca + 2H2O -> CaO2 + 2H2, C Ca + H2O -> CaOH + 1/2 H2, D Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2.
steps: Calcium reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Ca(OH)2 contains two OH- ions per Ca2+, so two H2O molecules are needed.
A, B and C give incorrect products or are unbalanced.
Answer D.

questions.question: Which element is oxidised and which is reduced when calcium reacts with water?
questions.answer: Calcium is oxidised (0 to +2); hydrogen is reduced (+1 to 0)
steps: Calcium goes from 0 in Ca to +2 in Ca(OH)2, so it loses electrons and is oxidised.
Hydrogen goes from +1 in H2O to 0 in H2, so it gains electrons and is reduced.

questions.question: What reagent and what result of the gas test show the presence of ammonium ions? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: NaOH(aq); damp red litmus paper turns blue
steps: Warming ammonium ions with a strong base (NaOH(aq)) gives ammonia gas: NH4+ + OH- -> NH3 + H2O.
Ammonia is alkaline, so it turns damp red litmus paper blue.
HCl(aq) would not release ammonia, so A and B are wrong; blue litmus turning red indicates an acidic gas, so C is wrong.

questions.question: What produces the colour in a flame test? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: energy emitted as electrons move from an excited state to the ground state
steps: The flame supplies energy, which excites electrons to higher energy levels.
When an excited electron falls back to a lower level (the ground state) it emits energy.
For some metal ions the energy emitted is in the visible region, giving the flame colour: option D.

questions.question: A titration adds dilute sulfuric acid from a burette to aqueous NaOH in a conical flask with methyl orange. What is the colour change at the end-point? A red to orange, B red to yellow, C yellow to orange, D yellow to red.
steps: Methyl orange is yellow in alkaline solution (the flask contains NaOH).
At the end-point, slight excess acid turns it orange.
So the colour change is yellow to orange.
Answer C.

questions.question: A student had an air bubble between the tap and tip of the burette, which filled with acid during the first titration. Which set of three titres could be the student's results? Options are in the PDF.
steps: The air bubble is displaced by acid, so the first reading drop is bigger than the volume that reached the flask: the first titre is too high.
The second and third titres are accurate, so they should be concordant with each other and smaller than the first.
C is the only row with a high first titre (22.80) and two concordant, lower values (22.35 and 22.40).
A has no high first titre (all three equal), B has second and third titres that are not concordant, and D has a first titre lower than the others.

questions.question: 25.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol dm-3 NaOH required a mean titre of 18.70 cm3 of sulfuric acid. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid? A 0.0374, B 0.0668, C 0.134, D 0.267 (mol dm-3).
steps: 2NaOH : 1 H2SO4, so moles H2SO4 = 0.00125 mol.
Concentration = 0.00125 / 0.01870 = 0.0668 mol dm-3.
Answer B.

questions.question: A titre of 13.25 cm3 was obtained using a 50 cm3 burette, where each reading has uncertainty +/-0.05 cm3. What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre? A +/-0.38%, B +/-0.75%, C +/-1.5%, D +/-7.5%.
steps: A titre uses two burette readings, so total uncertainty = 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.10 cm3.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.10 / 13.25 x 100 = 0.75%.
Answer B.

questions.question: A persistent yellow colour is seen when solid sodium chloride is placed in a Bunsen flame. The yellow colour is due to: A electrons excited and emitting yellow light on returning to ground state, B excited and emitting blue-violet light, C excited and absorbing yellow light, D excited and absorbing blue-violet light.
questions.answer: A - electrons excited to higher energy levels emitting yellow light on returning to the ground state
steps: Heat from the flame excites electrons to higher energy levels.
As they fall back to lower levels they emit light of a specific energy.
For sodium this energy corresponds to yellow light.
Answer A (emission, not absorption).

questions.question: A piece of sodium of mass 1.15 g reacts completely with water, and the solution is made up to 250.0 cm3. What is the concentration of the NaOH solution? A 0.025, B 0.050, C 0.100, D 0.200 (mol dm-3).
steps: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, so moles NaOH = 0.0500 mol.
Concentration = 0.0500 / 0.2500 = 0.200 mol dm-3.
Answer D.

questions.question: When lithium reacts with excess oxygen only lithium oxide forms, but sodium forms both sodium oxide and sodium peroxide. What is the main reason sodium peroxide forms? A sodium is more reactive, B sodium has lower first ionisation energy, C the sodium ion has a larger ionic radius, D the sodium ion has a higher charge density.
questions.answer: C - the sodium ion has a larger ionic radius
steps: The large peroxide ion, O2^2-, needs a large cation to stabilise it.
The Na+ ion is larger than Li+, so it has lower charge density and polarises the peroxide ion less.
Small Li+ has high charge density and stabilises only the oxide ion, O2-.
Answer C; option D is the opposite of what is true.

questions.question: Compound Q gives a red colour in a flame test and a white precipitate when aqueous potassium sulfate is added. What is Q? A LiCl, B NaNO3, C Sr(NO3)2, D BaCl2.
steps: Strontium gives a red flame; barium gives a green flame, so D is ruled out.
Sr2+ forms a white precipitate of SrSO4 with sulfate ions.
LiCl and NaNO3 do not give a white precipitate with sulfate.
Answer C.

questions.topic: Reaction With More Than One Product
questions.question: Which reaction produces more than one product? Options are in the PDF.
steps: Strontium reacts with water to give two products: strontium hydroxide and hydrogen (Sr + 2H2O -> Sr(OH)2 + H2).
A gives only MgO, B only CaCl2, and D only Ba(OH)2 (BaO + H2O -> Ba(OH)2).
So only C produces more than one product.

questions.question: 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2. A sample decomposed completely to give 1200 cm3 of gas at r.t.p. What mass of magnesium nitrate was used? A 1.48 g, B 2.97 g, C 7.42 g, D 14.8 g (Mr = 148.3; molar volume 24 000 cm3 mol-1).
steps: Moles of gas = 1200 / 24 000 = 0.0500 mol.
Every 2 mol Mg(NO3)2 give 5 mol gas, so moles Mg(NO3)2 = 0.0500 x 2 / 5 = 0.0200 mol.
Answer B.

questions.question: Discuss the thermal stability of the anhydrous nitrates of Groups 1 and 2. Explain the trend in thermal stability of Group 2 nitrates, describe differences in products of decomposition of Group 1 nitrates, and give equations for the decomposition of sodium nitrate and magnesium nitrate.
questions.answer: Group 2 nitrates become more stable down the group; Group 1 nitrates (except Li) give nitrite and O2; 2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2; 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2
steps: Group 2 nitrates decompose to the oxide, NO2 and O2; e.g. 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2.
Thermal stability of Group 2 nitrates increases down the group, as cation size increases and charge density falls.
Smaller cations with high charge density polarise the nitrate ion strongly, weakening N-O bonds and lowering the decomposition temperature.
Group 1 nitrates (except lithium) decompose to the nitrite and oxygen only: 2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2.
Lithium nitrate behaves like Group 2 nitrates, giving Li2O, NO2 and O2 because Li+ is small and highly polarising.
State that the NO2 produced in the Group 2 and lithium cases is brown and the nitrite products are colourless solids.

questions.question: Which property decreases as Group 2 is descended? A atomic radius, B reactivity of the elements, C solubility of the sulfates, D thermal stability of the nitrates.
steps: Atomic radius increases down Group 2 (A increases).
Reactivity increases down Group 2 (B increases).
Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2 (C decreases).
Thermal stability of nitrates increases down Group 2 (D increases). Answer C.

questions.question: Which statement is not explained by hydrogen bonding? A all Group 1 hydroxides are soluble in water, B many simple alcohols are soluble in water, C density of ice is less than liquid water at 0 C, D melting temperature of water is abnormally high.
questions.answer: A - all Group 1 hydroxides are soluble in water
steps: Solubility of Group 1 hydroxides is due to ionic lattice and hydration of ions, not hydrogen bonding.
Alcohol solubility is due to hydrogen bonds between alcohol and water (B is explained).
Ice has an open hydrogen-bonded lattice so is less dense (C is explained).
Water's high melting temperature is due to hydrogen bonds (D is explained). Answer A.

questions.question: Compound X gives a red flame test colour and a white precipitate when dilute HCl is added followed by barium chloride. Which compound is X? A calcium chloride, B lithium sulfate, C potassium sulfate, D strontium chloride.
steps: A white precipitate with BaCl2 after acid shows sulfate ions (BaSO4).
So X must be a sulfate: B or C.
Lithium gives a red flame, whereas potassium gives a lilac flame.
Answer B.

questions.question: Which process explains the flame colour produced by the compounds of Group 1 elements? A absorption as electrons are promoted, B absorption as electrons are removed, C emission as electrons return to lower energy levels, D emission as electrons are added to gaseous ions.
questions.answer: C - emission of visible light as electrons return to lower energy levels
steps: Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels.
When they drop back to lower levels they emit light of a fixed energy.
The energy of this light is in the visible range for Group 1 metals, giving the flame colour.
Answer C.

questions.question: Calculate the mass of ethanedioic acid needed to make 1000 cm3 of 0.0500 mol dm-3 solution. Molar mass = 90.0 g mol-1. Give the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
steps: Moles needed = 0.0500 mol dm-3 x 1.000 dm3 = 0.0500 mol.
Mass = moles x molar mass = 0.0500 x 90.0 = 4.50 g.
Give 3 significant figures, matching 0.0500 and 90.0.

questions.question: 400 cm3 of 0.0500 mol dm-3 ethanedioic acid has phenolphthalein added. Calculate the minimum mass of solid KOH needed to produce a colour change. Equation 2KOH + (COOH)2 -> (COOK)2 + 2H2O.
steps: Moles of ethanedioic acid = 0.0500 x 0.400 = 0.0200 mol.
From 2KOH : 1 acid, moles KOH needed = 0.0400 mol.
Mass KOH = 0.0400 x 56.1 = 2.24 g (the colour change occurs at equivalence, so this is the minimum).

questions.question: A student used 0.0500 mol dm-3 ethanedioic acid to find the accurate concentration of a KOH solution of approximate concentration. Describe a procedure to obtain reliable titration results using standard laboratory equipment.
questions.answer: Use a pipette to measure 25.0 cm3 of acid into a clean flask, add indicator, titrate with KOH from a burette to the first permanent colour change, repeat until concordant titres, then take the mean
steps: Rinse the burette with KOH solution and the pipette with the ethanedioic acid before use, then fill and set the burette to zero.
Pipette an accurate 25.0 cm3 of ethanedioic acid into a clean conical flask and add a few drops of phenolphthalein.
Add KOH slowly from the burette, swirling, until the first permanent colour change (colourless to pink); read the burette at eye level.
Record the titre to 0.05 cm3, then repeat until at least two titres agree within about 0.10 cm3 (concordant).
Use a white tile under the flask to see the colour change clearly and rinse the flask with distilled water between runs.
Calculate the mean of the concordant titres and use it in the calculation to reduce random error.

questions.question: A colourless solid Q was warmed with NaOH solution. A gas was evolved which turned damp red litmus blue. What is Q? A NaNO3, B NH4Cl, C NaCl, D Ca(NO3)2.
steps: A gas that turns damp red litmus blue is alkaline: ammonia.
Ammonia is released when an ammonium salt is warmed with NaOH.
Only NH4Cl contains the ammonium ion, NH4+.
Answer B.

questions.question: Which statement about trends going down Group 2 is correct? A thermal stability of nitrates decreases, B thermal stability of carbonates decreases, C solubility of hydroxides increases, D solubility of sulfates increases.
steps: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates increases down Group 2 (A and B are wrong).
Solubility of hydroxides increases down Group 2 (C is correct).
Solubility of sulfates decreases down Group 2 (D is wrong).
Answer C.

questions.question: A white solid gives a red flame test and produces a colourless, acidic gas when heated. What is the compound? A calcium carbonate, B calcium nitrate, C sodium carbonate, D strontium nitrate.
steps: A colourless acidic gas on heating is CO2, so the compound is a carbonate.
Nitrates give brown NO2, so B and D are ruled out.
Sodium carbonate gives a yellow flame, but calcium gives a red (brick-red) flame.
Answer A.

questions.question: Which statement about Group 2 is true? A calcium hydroxide is less soluble than magnesium hydroxide, B all Group 2 metals give a characteristic flame colour, C magnesium carbonate does not thermally decompose, D the first ionisation energy of magnesium is greater than that of calcium.
questions.answer: D - the first ionisation energy of magnesium is greater than that of calcium
steps: Calcium hydroxide is more soluble than magnesium hydroxide (A false).
Magnesium gives no characteristic flame colour (B false).
Magnesium carbonate decomposes on heating to MgO and CO2 (C false).
Mg has a smaller atomic radius and a higher nuclear charge than Ca, so its first ionisation energy is greater (D true).

questions.question: Write an equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of lithium with water to form lithium hydroxide solution.
steps: Lithium reacts with water to give LiOH and hydrogen gas.
Balance Li with 2 atoms each side and H/O with 2 H2O.
LiOH is aqueous (soluble) and H2 is a gas.
Equation: 2Li(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2LiOH(aq) + H2(g).

questions.question: Give two observations made during the reaction of lithium with water.
questions.answer: Effervescence (bubbles of hydrogen gas); the lithium floats and moves about on the surface and gets smaller as it dissolves
steps: Lithium is less dense than water, so it floats on the surface.
Hydrogen gas is produced, giving bubbles or fizzing.
The lithium gets smaller and dissolves, forming a solution.
Any two of these observations gain both marks.

questions.question: State how lithium nitride is formed when lithium metal tarnishes in air, including the formula of lithium nitride.
questions.answer: Lithium reacts directly with nitrogen from the air: 6Li + N2 -> 2Li3N; formula Li3N
steps: Lithium is highly reactive and reacts with nitrogen gas in the air at room temperature.
Lithium forms the nitride ion N3-, so each N needs three Li+ ions.
Formula of lithium nitride is Li3N.
Equation: 6Li + N2 -> 2Li3N.

questions.question: The cell has an anode of C6Li and a cathode of CoO2; Li atoms lose electrons at the anode and CoO2 combines with Li+ and electrons at the cathode to form LiCoO2. Give the overall equation when the cell is used (no state symbols).
steps: Anode: C6Li -> 6C + Li+ + e-.
Cathode: CoO2 + Li+ + e- -> LiCoO2.
Add the half-equations so the electrons and Li+ cancel.
Overall: C6Li + CoO2 -> 6C + LiCoO2.

questions.question: Describe, with reference to oxidation numbers, what happens to Co when the cell is in use.
questions.answer: Co is reduced from +4 in CoO2 to +3 in LiCoO2 (it gains an electron)
steps: In CoO2, O = -2 each, so Co = +4.
In LiCoO2, Li = +1 and O = -2 each, so Co = +3.
The oxidation number of Co decreases from +4 to +3.
A decrease in oxidation number means cobalt is reduced (it gains electrons).

questions.question: Suggest one property the separator must have to ensure the lithium battery is viable.
questions.answer: It must be permeable to Li+ ions but electrically insulating, so electrons cannot pass through it
steps: The separator keeps the electrodes apart so they cannot short-circuit.
It must let Li+ ions pass through to complete the circuit.
It must not conduct electrons, so electrons travel through the external circuit.
Any one of these properties gains the mark.

questions.question: An aluminium-lithium alloy contains 2.45% Li by mass and the rest Al. Calculate the molar ratio Al : Li in this alloy.
steps: Assume 100 g of alloy: Li = 2.45 g, Al = 97.55 g.
Divide by the smaller value: Al : Li = 3.61 / 0.355 = 10.2.
So the molar ratio Al : Li is 10.2 : 1, about 10 : 1.

questions.question: Suggest a reason why this alloy is better than pure aluminium for aircraft manufacture.
questions.answer: The alloy is less dense (lighter) and stronger than pure aluminium
steps: Lithium has a very low density, so adding it lowers the density of the alloy.
A lighter aircraft uses less fuel.
The alloy is also harder and stronger than pure aluminium.
Either a lower density or greater strength gains the mark.

questions.question: Explain why the ionic radii of Li+ and Mg2+ are similar, and why the thermal decomposition of lithium nitrate is similar to that of magnesium nitrate but different from sodium nitrate. Include equations.
questions.answer: Li+ and Mg2+ are similar in size (diagonal relationship: Mg2+ has a greater nuclear charge but also more charge); Li and Mg nitrates decompose to oxide, NO2 and O2, while NaNO3 gives nitrite and O2
steps: Li+ and Mg2+ are isoelectronic (1s2 configuration) and have similar sizes; Mg2+ has a larger nuclear charge that pulls its electrons closer, offsetting its extra positive charge.
So Li+ and Mg2+ have similar charge densities, which explains their similar chemical behaviour (diagonal relationship).
Lithium nitrate decomposes: 4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2, like magnesium nitrate: 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2.
Both Li+ and Mg2+ have high charge density, so they polarise the nitrate ion strongly, weakening N-O bonds and forming oxides.
Sodium nitrate has a larger, lower charge density Na+, which polarises the nitrate less: 2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2.
So lithium and magnesium nitrates give NO2 and an oxide, while sodium nitrate gives nitrite and oxygen only.

questions.question: State how you could ensure that all the water has been removed from hydrated magnesium sulfate crystals when heating.
questions.answer: Heat to constant mass: repeatedly heat, cool in a desiccator and weigh until the mass no longer changes
steps: Heat the crystals, then allow them to cool (ideally in a desiccator) before weighing.
Reheat and reweigh until two successive masses agree.
A constant mass shows that all the water of crystallisation has been removed.

questions.question: The mass of hydrated magnesium sulfate fell from 6.92 g to 6.04 g on heating. Mr MgSO4 = 120.4. Calculate the number of water molecules, x, in MgSO4.xH2O.
steps: Mass of water lost = 6.92 - 6.04 = 0.88 g.
Moles of water = 0.88 / 18.0 = 0.0489 mol.
Moles of MgSO4 = 6.04 / 120.4 = 0.0502 mol.
Ratio water : MgSO4 = 0.0489 / 0.0502 = 0.97, which rounds to 1, so x = 1.

questions.question: 100.0 g of water was used to dissolve 0.0628 mol of anhydrous MgSO4. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution, with sign and units (specific heat capacity 4.18 J g-1 C-1; density 1.00 g cm-3). The temperature results are in a table in the PDF.
steps: Temperature rise = 29.4 - 16.6 = 12.8 deg C.
Heat = m c Delta T = 100.0 g x 4.18 J g-1 deg C-1 x 12.8 = 5350 J = 5.35 kJ.
Moles of MgSO4 = 0.0628, so energy per mole = 5.35 / 0.0628 = 85.2 kJ mol^-1.
The temperature rose, so the dissolving is exothermic: Delta H = -85.2 kJ mol^-1 (3 significant figures, as the data).

questions.question: Complete the Hess cycle for the dissolving of hydrated magnesium sulfate MgSO4.7H2O (second experiment).
questions.answer: Bottom box: MgSO4(aq); arrows from both top boxes down to it, labelled -85.2 kJ mol^-1 (left) and +15.8 kJ mol^-1 (right)
steps: Both MgSO4(s) + 7H2O(l) and MgSO4.7H2O(s) can be dissolved to give the same final state, MgSO4(aq).
Write MgSO4(aq) in the empty bottom box.
Draw an arrow from MgSO4(s) + 7H2O(l) down to MgSO4(aq), labelled with the result from (b)(i): Delta H = -85.2 kJ mol^-1.
Draw an arrow from MgSO4.7H2O(s) down to MgSO4(aq), labelled Delta H = +15.8 kJ mol^-1.

questions.question: Using the completed Hess cycle and the answer to (b)(i), calculate the enthalpy change when anhydrous MgSO4 forms MgSO4.7H2O.
steps: By Hess's Law, the top arrow (anhydrous + 7H2O -> hydrated) plus the dissolving of the hydrated salt equals dissolving the anhydrous salt directly.
Delta H(top arrow) + (+15.8) = -85.2.
Delta H(top arrow) = -85.2 - 15.8 = -101.0 kJ mol^-1 (exothermic).

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram showing how both the magnesium ion and the sulfate ion interact with water molecules.
questions.answer: Mg2+ surrounded by water molecules with the O (delta-) end pointing at it; SO4 2- surrounded by water molecules with H (delta+) pointing at the O atoms of the ion
steps: Draw Mg2+ with several water molecules around it, each with its O atom (delta-, lone pair) nearest the ion; label the attraction as ion-dipole bonds (dotted lines).
Draw SO4 2- with several water molecules around it, each with its H atoms (delta+) pointing towards the O atoms of the sulfate ion; label these as ion-dipole attractions (hydrogen bonds).
Mark the charges 2+ and 2- on the ions and delta+ / delta- on the water molecules, and label the water molecules.

questions.question: Describe how drinking magnesium sulfate solution reduces the extent of barium poisoning, and include an ionic equation with state symbols.
questions.answer: Sulfate ions in the drink react with barium ions in the stomach to form insoluble BaSO4, which is not absorbed: Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s)
steps: Barium ions are toxic because they are absorbed from the gut when in solution.
Magnesium sulfate supplies SO4^2- ions in the stomach.
These react with Ba2+ ions to form insoluble barium sulfate, which is not absorbed into the blood.
Ionic equation: Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s).

questions.question: Steam is passed over heated magnesium. Which reaction occurs most readily? A Mg + H2O -> MgO + H2, B Mg + 2H2O -> Mg(OH)2 + H2, C 2Mg + H2O -> Mg2O + H2, D 2Mg + 2H2O -> 2MgOH + H2.
steps: Magnesium reacts with steam at high temperature to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen.
Mg(OH)2 is not formed from steam, since hot steam gives the oxide.
Option A is balanced: 1 Mg, 1 O, 2 H on each side.
Options C and D contain incorrect formulae (Mg2O, MgOH). Answer A.

questions.question: 10.00 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid is neutralised by 25.00 cm3 of 0.80 mol dm-3 KOH with methyl orange. What is the colour change at the end-point? A orange to red, B red to orange, C orange to yellow, D yellow to orange.
steps: The flask contains acid, so methyl orange starts red.
Potassium hydroxide from the burette neutralises the acid.
At the end-point methyl orange changes from red to orange (in a near neutral solution).
Answer B.

questions.question: What is the concentration of the potassium sulfate produced at the end-point, to 2 significant figures? A 0.010, B 0.020, C 0.29, D 0.57 (mol dm-3).
steps: 2KOH + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2H2O, so moles K2SO4 = 0.0100 mol.
Concentration = 0.0100 / 0.03500 = 0.29 mol dm-3.

questions.question: Information about the uncertainties in each reading used to measure the volumes is given in a table in the PDF. Which statement is true? Options A to D are in the PDF.
questions.answer: C: the total percentage uncertainty is 0.8 %
steps: Percentage uncertainty = (uncertainty / volume) x 100.
Sulfuric acid, 10.00 cm3 from a pipette: 0.04 / 10.00 x 100 = 0.4 %.
Potassium hydroxide, 25.00 cm3 from a burette: the volume is the difference of two readings, so uncertainty = 2 x 0.05 = 0.10 cm3, and 0.10 / 25.00 x 100 = 0.4 %.
Total = 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8 %, so C. A is wrong (the two are equal), B is wrong (0.4 %, not 0.8 %), and D is wrong (0.2 % uses only one burette reading).

questions.question: A 20 g sample of Fe2(SO4)3 (Mr = 400) is dissolved in water. How many sulfate ions are in the solution? Avogadro constant = 6.0 x 10^23 mol-1. A 3 x 10^22, B 9 x 10^22, C 1.2 x 10^23, D 1.5 x 10^23.
steps: Each formula unit contains 3 sulfate ions, so moles SO4^2- = 0.150 mol.
Number of ions = 0.150 x 6.0 x 10^23 = 9 x 10^22.
Answer B.

questions.question: Give the complete electronic configuration, using s, p, d notation, of a calcium atom in its ground state.
steps: Calcium has atomic number 20, so it has 20 electrons.
Fill orbitals in order: 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p6, 4s2.
Count: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 20 electrons.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers, why Ca(s) + Cl2(g) -> CaCl2(s) is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: Ca is oxidised from 0 to +2, and Cl is reduced from 0 to -1 in CaCl2, so it is redox
steps: Ca changes from 0 in the element to +2 in CaCl2, so it is oxidised.
Each Cl changes from 0 in Cl2 to -1 in CaCl2, so it is reduced.
Both oxidation and reduction occur, so the reaction is redox.

questions.question: Complete the table to show the type(s) of bonding and structure in the species involved in Ca(s) + Cl2(g) -> CaCl2(s).
questions.answer: Ca: metallic bonding, giant metallic lattice; Cl2: covalent bonding, simple molecular; CaCl2: ionic bonding, giant ionic lattice
steps: Calcium is a metal, so it has metallic bonding and a giant metallic lattice.
Cl2 is a non-metal molecule, so the bonding within the molecule is covalent and the structure is simple molecular.
CaCl2 is a metal bonded to a non-metal, so it has ionic bonding and a giant ionic lattice.
Fill in one bonding type and one structure for each of the three species.

questions.question: State the expected flame colour when CaCl2 is used in a flame test.
steps: Calcium ions give a characteristic brick-red flame.
The chloride ion does not change the flame colour.

questions.question: A sample of solid anhydrous calcium nitrate is heated strongly for several minutes in an apparatus. State two observations.
questions.answer: A brown gas (NO2) is given off, and a white solid (CaO) remains; oxygen may relight a glowing splint
steps: Ca(NO3)2 decomposes on strong heating to CaO, NO2 and O2.
Observation 1: brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide are seen.
Observation 2: a white solid, calcium oxide, is left in the tube.
Oxygen gas is also released and would relight a glowing splint.

questions.question: Explain why the observations in (c)(i) would be made more quickly if the experiment was repeated with anhydrous magnesium nitrate.
questions.answer: Mg2+ has a higher charge density than Ca2+, so it polarises the nitrate ion more and the N-O bonds weaken, so decomposition occurs at a lower temperature and more quickly
steps: Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+, so it has a higher charge density.
A higher charge density polarises the nitrate ion more strongly.
This weakens the N-O bonds more, so decomposition happens more readily at a given temperature.
The NO2 and O2 are therefore produced more quickly.

questions.topic: Calcium And Magnesium In Cold Water
questions.question: Samples of calcium and magnesium are added to separate test tubes of cold water containing universal indicator. State and explain the differences in observations, including an equation.
questions.answer: Calcium reacts steadily with fizzing and the indicator turns strongly alkaline (purple/blue); magnesium reacts very slowly or hardly at all with cold water, so the indicator changes only slightly (green/blue-green)
steps: Calcium reacts with cold water steadily: Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2, giving bubbles of hydrogen.
Ca(OH)2 is soluble enough to give a high [OH-], so the universal indicator turns purple (pH about 12-13).
Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, so little or no gas is seen.
Mg(OH)2 is sparingly soluble and gives only a low [OH-], so the indicator changes only slightly (green/blue-green, pH about 9-10).
The difference is due to the greater reactivity of calcium (larger atomic radius, lower ionisation energy) compared with magnesium.
Magnesium reacts readily only with steam, not with cold water.

questions.question: Group 2 compounds give different colours in a flame test. The best explanation is that the cations have different: A gaps between electronic energy levels, B ionic radii, C ionisation energies, D numbers of electrons.
questions.answer: A - gaps between electronic energy levels
steps: Flame colours come from electrons falling between energy levels.
Each metal ion has its own energy level gaps, giving light of a particular colour.
Ionic radius and ionisation energy do not determine the colour.
Answer A.

questions.question: Which test reagent could be used to identify an aqueous solution containing hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO3-? A sodium carbonate, B sodium hydroxide, C nitric acid, D ammonia.
steps: Hydrogencarbonate reacts with acid: HCO3- + H+ -> CO2 + H2O.
The CO2 gas evolved (fizzing) identifies the hydrogencarbonate, which is confirmed by the limewater test.
Sodium carbonate, sodium hydroxide and ammonia do not give a characteristic gas with hydrogencarbonate.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which statement explains the origin of a flame test colour? A electrons absorb energy as they jump to a higher level, B electrons emit energy as they jump to a higher level, C electrons absorb energy as they drop to a lower level, D electrons emit energy as they drop to a lower level.
questions.answer: D - electrons emit energy as they drop to a lower energy level
steps: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels (they absorb energy).
When electrons drop back to lower levels they emit energy as light.
This emitted light gives the flame colour.
Answer D.

questions.question: What are the products formed when lithium nitrate and calcium nitrate are heated separately? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: lithium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen; calcium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen
steps: Group 2 nitrates decompose to the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: 2Ca(NO3)2 -> 2CaO + 4NO2 + O2.
Lithium is the exception in Group 1: its small ion has a high charge density, so it polarises the nitrate ion strongly, and it behaves like Group 2: 4LiNO3 -> 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2.

Other Group 1 nitrates give a nitrite and oxygen only, but lithium nitrate does not, and calcium nitrate does not give a nitrite, so rows A, B and C (each has a nitrite for lithium or calcium) are wrong.
So both give oxide, NO2 and O2: row D.

questions.question: 25.0 cm3 of 0.205 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid was titrated with NaOH; the titre was 14.60 cm3. What is the concentration of the NaOH? A 0.176, B 0.239, C 0.351, D 0.702 (mol dm-3).
steps: 2NaOH : 1 H2SO4, so moles NaOH = 0.01025 mol.
Concentration NaOH = 0.01025 / 0.01460 = 0.702 mol dm-3.
Answer D.

questions.question: The burette is accurate to 0.05 cm3 per reading. What is the percentage error in the titre of 14.60 cm3? A 0.10%, B 0.34%, C 0.40%, D 0.68%.
steps: Two burette readings each +/-0.05 cm3, so the titre error is 0.10 cm3.
Percentage error = 0.10 / 14.60 x 100 = 0.68%.
Answer D.

questions.question: A graph shows the decomposition temperature (K) of Group 2 nitrates against atomic number. Estimate the temperature in C at which calcium nitrate decomposes. Options A 587 C, B 767 C, C 860 C, D 1040 C.
steps: Calcium has atomic number 20, so read the graph at 20 on the x-axis.
The curve is at about 860 K there (just below the 900 K line).
Convert to deg C: 860 - 273 = 587 deg C, which is option A.
Option C (860 deg C) wrongly treats the reading in K as deg C.

questions.question: Which order is correct for the solubilities of Group 2 sulfates? A barium > strontium > magnesium, B calcium > strontium > magnesium, C magnesium > barium > calcium, D calcium > strontium > barium.
steps: Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2, so Ca > Sr > Ba.
Mg sulfate is very soluble, but it is not part of the Ca, Sr, Ba order in D.
Options A, B and C give wrong orders for the sulfates.
Answer D.

questions.question: 20 cm3 of saturated barium nitrate at 80 C was cooled to 20 C, and 9.32 g of crystals precipitated. Solubility at 20 C is 3.74 g per 100 g water. What is the solubility at 80 C in g per 100 g water? A 13.1, B 41.0, C 46.6, D 50.3.
steps: Take 20 cm3 of the saturated solution to contain 20 g of water (density taken as 1.00 g cm-3: an assumption needed to use the data given).
At 20 deg C that 20 g of water holds 3.74 x (20/100) = 0.748 g of barium nitrate, so 0.748 g stays dissolved.
At 80 deg C the 20 g of water held 9.32 + 0.748 = 10.068 g.
Per 100 g of water: 10.068 x 5 = 50.3 g (D). Option C (46.6) comes from forgetting the 0.748 g that stays in solution.

questions.question: What is the flame colour produced by strontium ions? A green, B red, C white, D yellow.
steps: Strontium ions give a red flame.
Barium gives green, sodium yellow and calcium brick-red.
Answer B.

questions.topic: Gas Volume From Ideal Gas Law
questions.question: One mole of magnesium nitrate is completely decomposed (2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2). What is the maximum volume of gas at 600 K and 101 000 Pa? [R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1] A 0.025 m3, B 0.099 m3, C 0.123 m3, D 0.247 m3.
steps: 1 mol Mg(NO3)2 gives 2 mol NO2 + 0.5 mol O2 = 2.5 mol gas.
Use pV = nRT, so V = nRT / p = 2.5 x 8.31 x 600 / 101 000.
Answer C.

questions.question: What is the percentage yield if 25.0 g of magnesium oxide is produced from one mole of magnesium nitrate? [Mr MgO = 40.3] A 13.6%, B 16.9%, C 31.0%, D 62.0%.
steps: 1 mol Mg(NO3)2 gives 1 mol MgO (2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO).
Theoretical mass of MgO = 1 x 40.3 = 40.3 g.
Percentage yield = 25.0 / 40.3 x 100 = 62.0%.
Answer D.

questions.question: What is the concentration, in mol dm-3, when 64.5 g of NaNO3 (Mr 85.0) is dissolved in water to form 750 cm3 of solution? A 0.086, B 0.113, C 0.759, D 1.012.
steps: Volume = 750 cm3 = 0.750 dm3.
Concentration = 0.7588 / 0.750 = 1.012 mol dm-3.
Answer D.

questions.question: 10.0 cm3 of magnesium chloride solution gave 0.398 g of magnesium hydroxide precipitate (Mr 58.3) with excess NaOH. What was the concentration of the MgCl2 solution? A 0.00683, B 0.0137, C 0.683, D 1.37 (mol dm-3).
steps: Mg2+ : Mg(OH)2 is 1:1, so moles MgCl2 = 0.00683 mol.
Concentration = 0.00683 / 0.0100 = 0.683 mol dm-3.
Answer C.

questions.question: Calcium carbonate is heated to give calcium oxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. What is the atom economy by mass for the formation of calcium oxide? A 44.0%, B 56.0%, C 78.6%, D 100%.
steps: Atom economy = Mr of desired product / Mr of all products x 100.
Mr CaO = 40.1 + 16.0 = 56.1; Mr CO2 = 44.0; total of products = 100.1.
Answer B.

questions.question: 25 cm3 of 2.00 mol dm-3 NaOH is added to 30 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 ethanoic acid in a polystyrene cup; the temperature rises by 6.5 C. Assume specific heat capacity 4.18 J g-1 C-1 and density 1.00 g cm-3. Which expression gives the enthalpy of neutralisation in J mol-1? A -(25 x 4.18 x 6.5) x 0.05, B -(30 x 4.18 x 6.5) x 0.03, C -(55 x 4.18 x 6.5) x 0.05, D -(55 x 4.18 x 6.5) / 0.03.
steps: Total volume of mixture = 25 + 30 = 55 cm3, so mass = 55 g (density 1.00 g cm-3).
Heat released q = m x c x deltaT = 55 x 4.18 x 6.5 J.
Moles of water formed = limiting reagent = ethanoic acid = 1.00 x 0.030 = 0.030 mol (NaOH is in excess: 0.050 mol).
deltaH = -q / n = -(55 x 4.18 x 6.5) / 0.03 J mol-1, which is option D.
The 0.03 is the moles, so dividing by it gives J per mol.

questions.question: The thermometer has uncertainty +/-0.5 C for each reading. What is the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change of 6.5 C? A 3.8%, B 7.7%, C 15.4%, D 30.8%.
steps: Temperature change uses two readings, so total uncertainty = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 C.
Percentage uncertainty = 1.0 / 6.5 x 100 = 15.4%.
Answer C.

questions.question: Which electron movement causes the yellow colour in a sodium chloride flame test? A addition of an electron to a sodium ion, B an electron moving from 3p to 3s, C an electron moving from 3s to 3p, D removal of an electron from a sodium atom.
questions.answer: B - an electron moving from 3p to 3s
steps: The flame excites an electron from 3s up to 3p (absorbs energy).
The excited electron falls back from 3p to 3s, emitting light.
The energy of this 3p to 3s transition corresponds to yellow light.
Answer B.
